2.4.1    Gradient-Based Saliency Methods

Interpretability methods for neural networks can be classified along two axes: global
versus local, and gradient-based versus perturbation-based. Local gradient-based
methods explain individual predictions by computing the gradient of the output
score with respect to the input image, highlighting pixels that most influence the
prediction. Simonyan et al. [44] proposed the vanilla gradient approach, which

producing sharper and more spatially coherent saliency maps.

1.4.2.1 Minimization of the mean squared error.

We will consider as design criteria the squared error, c(e) = (s − ŝ)2 , so the optimal weight
vector will be the one that minimizes the MSE risk:

                        w∗ = argmin E{(S − Ŝ)2 } = argmin E{(S − w⊺ Z)2 }                          (1.57)
                                   w                             w

and we will refer to the estimator associated with the weight vector as ŜLMSE :

                                                ŜLMSE = w∗ T Z

   The MSE can be expanded as

                             MSE = E{(S − Ŝ)2 } = E{(S − w⊺ Z)2 }
                                     = E{S2 } − 2E{w⊺ ZS} + E{(w⊺ Z)2 }
                                     = E{S2 } − 2E{SZ}⊺ w + w⊺ E{ZZ⊺ }w
                                     = E{S2 } − 2r⊺SZ w + w⊺ RZ w                                   (1.58)

where
• rSZ = E{SZ} is the cross-correlation vector between S and Z
• RZ = E{ZZ⊺ } is the autocorrelation matrix of Z.
Thus, the MSE is a second-degree polynomial in w. This is illustrated in Figure 1.6, which
depicts the error surface in a case with two observations. Being the function to minimize
quadratic in weights (minimization argument), the error surface will take the form of a N
dimensional paraboloid.




Fig. 1.6 Surface of the MSE for the linear estimator with Z = X, as a function of the parameters.
